Week 3 Overview

Where We Are in the ADM

Week 2 completed the design phases (A–E). This week covers:

  • The Preliminary Phase — which runs BEFORE Phase A and sets up the entire architecture practice
  • Phases F, G, H — where architecture moves from design into delivery and sustained management
  • Part III (ADM Techniques) — the tools architects use throughout the ADM
  • Part VII (Architecture Governance) — the governance structures that control architecture decisions
  • Part IV (Content Framework) — the taxonomy of what architecture produces

Understanding this material separates candidates who just know the ADM sequence from those who understand how TOGAF actually works in practice — and exam questions specifically test this distinction.

Exam Weight for Week 3 Content

Topic Approximate Exam Coverage
Preliminary Phase 5–8%
Phase F: Migration Planning 5–7%
Phase G: Implementation Governance 5–7%
Phase H: Architecture Change Management 5–7%
Architecture Governance (Part VII) 8–10%
ADM Techniques (Part III) 5–8%
Content Framework (Part IV) 8–10%
Total for Week 3 content ~40–55% of exam
Note

There is overlap with Week 2 content — architecture governance concepts appear throughout the exam, not just in governance-specific questions.

Study Schedule

Day Topic Study Time
Monday Preliminary Phase — Full Deep Dive 3 hours
Tuesday Phase F: Migration Planning 3 hours
Wednesday Phase G: Implementation Governance 3 hours
Thursday Phase H: Architecture Change Management 3 hours
Friday ADM Guidelines & Techniques (Part III) 3 hours
Saturday Architecture Governance (Part VII) + Content Framework (Part IV) 3 hours
Sunday Review + 30-Question Quiz 3 hours

Day 1: Preliminary Phase — Complete Deep Dive

What the Preliminary Phase Is

The Preliminary Phase is the foundation of everything. It runs before any specific architecture project begins and answers the question: Is this organization capable of doing architecture, and what rules will govern how we do it?

Think of it this way:

  • Preliminary Phase — sets up the kitchen: equipment, recipes, roles, quality standards
  • Phase A–H — cooking a specific meal in that kitchen

If the Preliminary Phase is poorly done, every architecture project that follows will suffer from inconsistent standards, unclear governance, and chaotic decision-making.

The Preliminary Phase is often run once when an organization first adopts TOGAF, then revisited when there are significant organizational changes, new stakeholder requirements, or major framework updates.

Formal Objectives of the Preliminary Phase

  1. Determine the Architecture Capability the organization requires and has
  2. Establish the Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture — who does what, with what budget
  3. Establish Architecture Principles — the governance rules for all future architecture decisions
  4. Tailor the TOGAF framework to fit the organization's culture, methods, and terminology
  5. Select and implement Architecture Tools — modeling tools, repositories, governance systems
  6. Establish the Architecture Governance Framework — how decisions are made and enforced

What Triggers the Preliminary Phase?

The Preliminary Phase is triggered by a commission from senior management — typically the Board of Directors, CEO, or CIO — to establish an enterprise architecture capability. This is different from a Request for Architecture Work (which triggers Phase A for a specific project).

The trigger is often framed as:

  • "We need a formal enterprise architecture practice"
  • "We've adopted TOGAF and need to set it up"
  • "We're going through a major transformation and need consistent architecture governance"

The Formal Steps of the Preliminary Phase (6 Steps)

Step 1: Scope the Enterprise Organizations Affected

  • Determine which parts of the enterprise will be included in the architecture program
  • Define the enterprise boundaries — which business units, geographies, subsidiaries
  • Identify what other frameworks are already in use (ITIL, COBIT, project management standards)
  • Determine the constraints: regulatory, financial, organizational
  • This scoping decision affects everything that follows — get it right here

Step 2: Confirm Governance and Support Frameworks

  • Identify existing governance structures (IT governance, corporate governance, risk management)
  • Understand how architecture governance will integrate with these existing frameworks
  • Establish how architecture decisions will be escalated and approved
  • Identify the sponsorship and commitment from senior leadership — without this, governance collapses

Step 3: Define and Establish Enterprise Architecture Team and Organization

  • Define the organizational structure for the EA function
  • Establish the Architecture Board (the governance body) — see Day 6 for details
  • Define roles: Chief Architect, Enterprise Architects, Domain Architects, Solution Architects
  • Establish budgets, reporting lines, and accountability for the EA function
  • This produces the Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture

Architecture Roles Hierarchy:

Chief Architect (strategic — leads the EA program)
    │
    ├── Enterprise Architect (organization-wide — spans all domains)
    │
    ├── Domain Architects (domain-specific)
    │   ├── Business Architect
    │   ├── Data Architect
    │   ├── Application Architect
    │   └── Technology Architect
    │
    └── Solution Architect (project-specific — designs solutions)
              (Note: Solution Architect is project-level; not strictly EA-level)
Exam tip

The Chief Architect leads the EA function. Domain Architects specialize in one of the 4 domains. Solution Architects work at project level. The Architecture Board is a governance body, not an individual role — it is a committee.

Step 4: Identify and Establish Architecture Principles

  • Architecture Principles are the fundamental rules that guide all architecture decisions in every ADM phase
  • Developed here in Preliminary Phase; applied throughout A–H
  • Each principle has exactly 4 components (heavily tested):
    • Name — short, memorable label (e.g., "Data is an Asset")
    • Statement — a clear, unambiguous declaration of the rule
    • Rationale — why the principle matters; business benefits of following it
    • Implications — what following the principle requires from business and IT

Example — Working Through All 4 Components:

Component Content
Name Technology Independence
Statement Applications shall not be dependent on specific hardware or operating system software
Rationale Reduces vendor lock-in; enables technology evolution without application rewrites; reduces long-term cost
Implications Requires abstraction layers in application design; increases initial development effort; may require middleware; vendor selection criteria must include open standards compliance

Categories of Architecture Principles: TOGAF organizes principles into categories:

  • Business Principles — govern business behavior (e.g., "Business Continuity", "Compliance with Law")
  • Data Principles — govern data management (e.g., "Data is an Asset", "Data is Accessible", "Data is Shared")
  • Application Principles — govern application design (e.g., "Technology Independence", "Ease-of-Use")
  • Technology Principles — govern technology choices (e.g., "Requirements-Based Change", "Responsive Change Management", "Control Technical Diversity")
Exam tip

Principles can be inherited from higher levels (e.g., corporate governance principles become architecture principles). Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase and confirmed/refined in Phase A. They must be explicitly applied in every subsequent phase.

Step 5: Tailor the TOGAF Framework

  • TOGAF is a framework, not a rigid prescription — it expects organizations to adapt it
  • Tailoring means: selecting which phases to use, adapting terminology, integrating with existing methods
  • The tailored version is called the Tailored Architecture Framework
  • Examples of tailoring:
    • Combining Phase F and Phase G for small organizations
    • Renaming "Architecture Board" to fit existing terminology
    • Adding organization-specific phases
    • Selecting which of TOGAF's techniques to use
    • Integrating TOGAF with PRINCE2, Agile, or SAFe
Exam tip

TOGAF explicitly allows and encourages tailoring. "Tailoring" is not a deviation or violation — it is a core feature. The tailored framework is a formal output of the Preliminary Phase.

Step 6: Implement Architecture Tools

  • Select and implement the modeling and repository tools that will support the EA practice
  • Examples: Sparx Enterprise Architect, Avolution ABACUS, Alfabet, BiZZdesign
  • Establish the Architecture Repository structure (6 layers: Metamodel, Capability, Landscape, Standards, Reference Library, Governance Log)
  • Configure governance processes in the tooling

Key Inputs to the Preliminary Phase

Input Source Why It Matters
TOGAF library The Open Group The framework being adopted
Other frameworks in use Organization Understand what already exists before adding TOGAF
Board strategies and business drivers Board / Executive Define why architecture is needed
Existing organizational model for EA Organization What already exists (if anything)
Existing governance frameworks Organization IT governance, legal frameworks, risk management
Existing architecture documentation Organization Baselines to build on

Key Outputs of the Preliminary Phase

Output What It Is Exam Importance
Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture Scope, roles, responsibilities, and budget for the EA function High
Tailored Architecture Framework TOGAF adapted to the organization, including tools and principles Very High
Architecture Principles The governance rules (with all 4 components) for all future decisions Very High
Initial Architecture Repository Populated with initial content and structure High
Architecture Governance Framework How decisions are made, who approves, escalation paths High
Restatement of Business Principles, Goals, Drivers Documented business context for the EA program Medium

Architecture Repository — The 6 Layers (Detailed)

The Architecture Repository is set up in the Preliminary Phase. It has 6 layers:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Layer 1: Architecture Metamodel                  │
│  (Rules for how artifacts are structured)         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 2: Architecture Capability                 │
│  (EA team: roles, skills, governance)             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 3: Architecture Landscape                  │
│  ├── Strategic Architecture (enterprise-wide)    │
│  ├── Segment Architecture (business unit-level)  │
│  └── Capability Architecture (enabling systems)  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 4: Standards Information Base              │
│  (Approved standards, technology standards)       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 5: Reference Library                       │
│  (Reference architectures, patterns, guidelines)  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 6: Governance Log                          │
│  (All architecture decisions, waivers, reviews)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Exam tip

The Governance Log (Layer 6) is where architecture decisions, dispensations (waivers), compliance results, and Architecture Board minutes are recorded. It is the permanent audit trail of the architecture governance function. Know this layer specifically — it appears in governance questions.

Preliminary Phase vs. Phase A — The Critical Distinction

Preliminary Phase Phase A
Runs Before any architecture project At the start of each architecture project
Triggered by Commission from senior management to establish EA Request for Architecture Work
Produces Architecture Principles, Governance Framework, Tailored Framework Architecture Vision, Statement of Architecture Work
Frequency Once (then periodically reviewed) Every architecture initiative
Scope The entire enterprise EA practice A specific architecture project
Analogy Setting up the kitchen Cooking a specific meal
Exam tip

This distinction is heavily tested. "Which phase establishes Architecture Principles?" → Preliminary. "Which phase produces the Statement of Architecture Work?" → Phase A. Never confuse the two.

Key Takeaway for Day 1 (Preliminary Phase)

The Preliminary Phase establishes the architecture capability — the ability to do architecture. Its most important outputs are Architecture Principles (with 4 components: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications), the Tailored Architecture Framework, and the Architecture Governance Framework. It runs before Phase A and is revisited whenever the architecture practice needs updating.

Day 2: Phase F — Migration Planning

What Phase F Is

Phase F is where the Architecture Roadmap and Implementation Plan produced in Phase E are finalized and made actionable. Phase F transforms the strategic output of Phase E (Version 0.1) into a detailed, approved, resource-committed plan ready for implementation.

The critical distinction (heavily tested):

Phase E Phase F
Focus WHAT to do and in what rough order HOW to do it: detailed schedule, costs, resources
Roadmap version Architecture Roadmap v0.1 Finalized Architecture Roadmap
Migration Plan version Implementation and Migration Plan v0.1 Implementation and Migration Plan (finalized)
Architecture Contracts Not yet created Created here — formal agreements for implementation
Level of planning Strategic Tactical and operational

Formal Objectives of Phase F

  1. Finalize the Architecture Roadmap across all 4 domains
  2. Ensure the Implementation and Migration Plan has sufficient detail for execution
  3. Assign business value to each Work Package — justify investment
  4. Create Architecture Contracts — formal implementation agreements
  5. Perform cost/benefit analysis and risk validation for each migration project
  6. Establish the Implementation Governance Model — how Phase G will oversee delivery

The Formal Steps of Phase F (7 Steps)

Phase F has 7 steps — different from the 9-step pattern of Phases B, C, D because Phase F is about planning, not architecture design:

Step 1: Confirm Management Framework Interactions for the Implementation and Migration Plan

  • Ensure the migration plan aligns with existing programme and project management frameworks in the organization (PRINCE2, PMI, SAFe, etc.)
  • Understand how the migration plan relates to business planning cycles, budgeting cycles, and governance calendars
  • This step prevents the architecture plan from being developed in isolation from how the organization actually manages projects

Step 2: Assign a Business Value to Each Work Package

  • Each Work Package must have a clearly articulated business value — not just technical necessity
  • Business value can be expressed as: cost savings, revenue increase, risk reduction, regulatory compliance, customer satisfaction improvement
  • Without business value assignment, the migration plan lacks the justification needed to secure and maintain executive support
  • Work Packages with low business value may be deprioritized or eliminated

Step 3: Estimate Resource Requirements, Project Timings, and Availability/Delivery Vehicle

  • Resource estimation: people, budget, tools, infrastructure needed for each Work Package
  • Project timings: when will each Work Package start and finish?
  • Delivery vehicle: how will the work be delivered? Options include:
    • In-house team
    • System integrator or consultancy
    • Software vendor
    • Outsourced delivery partner
    • Hybrid (mix of the above)
  • Identify resource conflicts: the same resource needed for multiple Work Packages at the same time

Step 4: Prioritize Migration Projects through Cost/Benefit Assessment and Risk Validation

  • For each Work Package: compare cost to business benefit
  • Validate risks identified in Phase E — are they still current? Have new risks emerged?
  • Prioritization criteria:
    • High value + low risk → implement first
    • High value + high risk → implement with mitigation
    • Low value + low risk → implement later
    • Low value + high risk → challenge whether to do at all
Prioritization Matrix:
              LOW RISK          HIGH RISK
HIGH VALUE  ┌─────────────┬─────────────────┐
            │ DO FIRST    │ DO WITH          │
            │ (Quick wins)│ MITIGATION       │
LOW VALUE   ├─────────────┼─────────────────┤
            │ DO LATER    │ QUESTION WHETHER │
            │ (Batch)     │ TO DO AT ALL     │
            └─────────────┴─────────────────┘

Step 5: Confirm Architecture Roadmap and Update Architecture Definition and Requirements

  • At this point, some refinements to the architecture may be needed based on planning realities
  • If resource or timing constraints mean some capabilities cannot be delivered, the target architecture may need adjustment
  • Update the Architecture Definition Document (ADD) and Architecture Requirements Specification if needed
  • This is the final opportunity to realign architecture with realistic constraints before committing to contracts

Step 6: Generate the Implementation and Migration Plan

  • This is the main deliverable of Phase F
  • The finalized plan includes:
    • Project start/end dates for all Work Packages
    • Resource assignments and budgets
    • Dependencies between Work Packages (critical path)
    • Milestones and governance checkpoints
    • Transition Architecture schedule — when each transition state is expected to be reached
    • Risk register with mitigation actions

Step 7: Complete the Architecture Development Cycle and Document Lessons Learned

  • Formally close the architecture development phase (Preliminary + A–F)
  • Document lessons learned from the architecture development process
  • What worked well? What would be done differently?
  • Lessons are stored in the Architecture Repository (Reference Library layer) for future ADM cycles
  • Formally hand over to Phase G (implementation governance)

Key Inputs to Phase F

Input Source
Architecture Roadmap v0.1 Phase E
Implementation and Migration Plan v0.1 Phase E
Work Package list Phase E
Transition Architectures Phase E
Architecture Definition Document (all 4 domains) Phases B, C, D
Architecture Requirements Specification Phases B, C, D
Capability Assessment Phase A / Phase E
Communications Plan Phase A

Key Outputs of Phase F

Output What It Is Exam Importance
Implementation and Migration Plan (finalized) Detailed, resource-committed plan for all Work Packages Very High
Finalized Architecture Roadmap Approved, sequenced roadmap Very High
Architecture Contracts Formal compliance agreements (see below) Very High
Finalized Architecture Definition Document ADD updated with any refinements High
Finalized Architecture Requirements Specification Updated if needed High
Implementation Governance Model Defines how Phase G will oversee delivery High
Lessons Learned document For future ADM cycles Medium

Architecture Contracts — Critical Concept

An Architecture Contract is a joint agreement between the development partners and sponsors on the deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose of an architecture.

What an Architecture Contract defines:

  • What will be delivered (deliverables and acceptance criteria)
  • Conformance to the architecture (which parts of the ADD must be followed)
  • Quality standards that must be met
  • Timescales and milestones
  • Responsibilities of each party
  • What happens if the architecture needs to change mid-delivery (change control process)
  • Signature of all parties — it is a formal binding agreement

Types of Architecture Contracts:

  1. Business Users' Architecture Contract — between the EA team and business stakeholders; covers business architecture conformance
  2. IT Architecture Contract — between the EA team and solution delivery teams; covers IS/Technology conformance
  3. Suppliers' Architecture Contract — between the organization and external vendors/system integrators; covers supplier delivery against the architecture

When Architecture Contracts are created: Phase F
When Architecture Contracts are enforced: Phase G
When Architecture Contracts may be amended: Phase H (if architecture changes)

Exam tip

Architecture Contracts are created in Phase F, NOT Phase G. Phase G enforces them. A common wrong answer is "Architecture Contracts are created during implementation" — this is incorrect.

Key Takeaway for Day 2 (Phase F)

Phase F finalizes the strategic outputs of Phase E into an actionable, resource-committed plan. Its most important outputs are the finalized Implementation and Migration Plan, the finalized Architecture Roadmap, and Architecture Contracts. Architecture Contracts are the key mechanism linking architecture design to implementation governance — created in Phase F, enforced in Phase G.

Day 3: Phase G — Implementation Governance

What Phase G Is

Phase G is where the architecture team governs the implementation — ensuring that what gets built matches what was designed. This is a critical phase because even perfect architecture design fails if the implementation deviates from it without proper control.

Phase G answers: Is the implementation following the architecture, and if it's deviating, is that deviation acceptable?

Key conceptual shift: In Phases A–F, architects are designing. In Phase G, architects are governing — reviewing, assessing, approving, and controlling. The architect's role changes from designer to overseer.

Formal Objectives of Phase G

  1. Ensure implementation projects comply with the agreed architecture
  2. Perform Compliance Assessments — formal evaluations of conformance
  3. Manage Architecture Change Requests that arise during implementation
  4. Guide solution deployment to ensure architecture intent is realized
  5. Close the implementation and hand over to Phase H (ongoing operations)

The Formal Steps of Phase G (6 Steps)

Step 1: Confirm Scope and Priorities for Deployment with Development Management

  • Review the Implementation and Migration Plan with project delivery teams
  • Confirm which Work Packages are starting and what the current priorities are
  • Establish the governance relationship between the EA team and each project team
  • This step is about establishing the working relationship — not designing anything

Step 2: Identify Deployment Resources and Skills

  • Confirm that the resources committed in Phase F are actually available
  • Identify skill gaps in implementation teams that could compromise architecture conformance
  • Arrange architecture support for implementation teams (architecture working sessions, design reviews)

Step 3: Guide Development of Solutions Deployment

  • Provide architecture guidance to implementation projects throughout delivery
  • This is proactive — architects work WITH projects, not just review them at the end
  • Review solution designs as they emerge
  • Provide interpretation of the Architecture Definition Document when teams have questions
  • Identify emerging issues early, before they become expensive problems

Step 4: Perform Enterprise Architecture Compliance Reviews

  • This is the most important step of Phase G
  • A Compliance Review is a formal assessment of how well a project's solution conforms to the architecture
  • Can be formal (Architecture Board review) or informal (lightweight desk review)
  • Reviews can occur at project milestones, at architecture decision points, or on a scheduled basis
  • Output: Compliance Assessment document

Architecture Compliance Levels: TOGAF defines architecture compliance on a spectrum from strongest to weakest:

Level Meaning
Fully Conformant The solution fully conforms to the architecture in all relevant respects
Conformant The solution conforms to the architecture across all relevant aspects
Compliant Some aspects of the architecture are not addressed by the solution, but it does not conflict
Consistent The solution uses the same terminology and concepts but has no direct relationship to the architecture
Irrelevant The architecture is not relevant to this solution
Non-conformant The solution deviates from or conflicts with the architecture
Exam tip

Know these 6 levels and their order from strongest to weakest: Fully Conformant > Conformant > Compliant > Consistent > Irrelevant > Non-conformant. The most dangerous is Non-conformant — it means there is an active conflict with the architecture that must be resolved.

What happens when a solution is Non-conformant? Options:

  1. Change the solution — redesign the implementation to conform
  2. Request a Dispensation (Waiver) — formally request permission to deviate (see Day 6: Architecture Governance)
  3. Revise the architecture — if the non-conformance reveals an architecture flaw, update the architecture (triggers a formal architecture change request)

Step 5: Implement Business and IT Operations

  • Support the transition of the new solution into live business and IT operations
  • Ensure business processes are updated to reflect the new architecture
  • Ensure IT operations teams have the knowledge and tools to support the new systems
  • Ensure training and change management activities are completed

Step 6: Perform Post-Implementation Review and Close the Implementation

  • After each Work Package is delivered, perform a Post-Implementation Review (PIR)
  • Was the architecture realized as designed?
  • Were the business benefits achieved?
  • What lessons can be captured for future projects?
  • Formally close the Work Package and update the Architecture Repository
  • When all Work Packages are complete, formally close Phase G and transition to Phase H

Key Inputs to Phase G

Input Source
Architecture Contracts Phase F — the compliance agreements to enforce
Architecture Definition Document Phases B, C, D (finalized in Phase F)
Architecture Requirements Specification Phases B, C, D (finalized in Phase F)
Implementation and Migration Plan Phase F
Architecture Governance Framework Preliminary Phase
Architecture Repository Ongoing

Key Outputs of Phase G

Output What It Is Exam Importance
Compliance Assessments Formal evaluations of project conformance to architecture Very High
Architecture Change Requests Formal proposals for changes to the architecture raised during implementation Very High
Implementation and Migration Plan (updated) Status-updated plan reflecting actual progress High
Architecture-compliant implemented system The delivered solution (the actual outcome) High
Architecture Contract (signed and monitored) Enforced and updated as needed High
Governance Log updates Records of all compliance decisions Medium
Post-Implementation Review Assessment of delivered value Medium

Phase G and the Architecture Board

The Architecture Board plays a critical role in Phase G:

  • Reviews Compliance Assessments for significant deviations
  • Approves or rejects Architecture Change Requests
  • Grants Dispensations (waivers) when solutions cannot conform
  • Records all decisions in the Governance Log
Exam tip

In Phase G, the architect does NOT redesign the architecture. Changes to the architecture come through formal Architecture Change Requests, approved by the Architecture Board. Architects cannot unilaterally change the architecture during implementation.

Key Takeaway for Day 3 (Phase G)

Phase G governs implementation — it does not design architecture. The key tool is the Compliance Assessment, which measures how well a project conforms to the architecture across 6 levels (Fully Conformant → Non-conformant). Architecture Contracts from Phase F are enforced here. Non-conformances are resolved by changing the solution, requesting a Dispensation, or formally revising the architecture via the Architecture Board.

Day 4: Phase H — Architecture Change Management

What Phase H Is

Phase H is where the deployed architecture is monitored and managed over time. Unlike Phases A–G, which are episodic (they run for a project and complete), Phase H is continuous — it runs indefinitely after implementation.

Phase H answers: Is the architecture still fit for purpose as the business and technology change, and how do we manage changes to it?

Phase H is not passive monitoring. It is active management of change requests, technology triggers, and business evolution — making decisions about what to do when the world changes.

Formal Objectives of Phase H

  1. Monitor the deployed architecture for drift — has the implementation deviated from the architecture baseline over time?
  2. Monitor the business and technology environment for changes that affect the architecture
  3. Evaluate Change Requests — formal proposals to modify the architecture
  4. Decide whether changes require a full new ADM cycle or can be handled within Phase H
  5. Maintain architecture compliance through ongoing governance
  6. Manage the Architecture Contract portfolio as systems evolve

What Triggers Activity in Phase H

Phase H activity is not triggered by a single event — it is ongoing. However, specific activities are triggered by:

Technology Triggers:

  • New technology emerges that offers significant advantages (e.g., a new cloud platform, AI/ML capability)
  • Existing technology approaches end-of-life (vendor withdraws support)
  • Security vulnerabilities discovered in deployed technology components
  • Technology standards change (e.g., a protocol is deprecated)

Business Triggers:

  • New business strategy (e.g., merger, acquisition, new market entry)
  • Regulatory or compliance changes (new privacy law, new financial regulation)
  • Business performance falling short of KPIs set in the Architecture Vision
  • New business capability needed that wasn't in the original target architecture

Architecture Triggers:

  • Implementation projects have made undocumented changes during Phase G
  • Lessons learned from delivery reveal gaps or errors in the architecture
  • The Architecture Board decides a periodic architecture review is due

The Formal Steps of Phase H (7 Steps)

Step 1: Establish Value Realization Process

  • Define how the business value promised in the Architecture Vision and Phase F will be measured and tracked
  • Set up monitoring of business KPIs and architecture KPIs
  • Example: if the architecture promised a 30% reduction in data processing time, establish how this will be measured

Step 2: Deploy Monitoring Tools

  • Implement the technical tools needed to monitor the deployed architecture
  • This includes: system performance monitoring, capacity monitoring, security monitoring, configuration management
  • The goal is early detection of drift — when deployed systems start deviating from the architecture baseline

Step 3: Manage Risks

  • Review the risk register from earlier phases — which risks have materialized? Which have been mitigated?
  • Identify new risks introduced by the deployed architecture
  • Update risk classifications and mitigation strategies
  • Escalate high-severity risks to the Architecture Board

Step 4: Provide Analysis for Architecture Change Management

  • When change requests or triggers are received, analyze their impact on the architecture
  • Impact analysis: what else would change if this request is approved?
  • This analysis is the basis for the decision in Step 7 (whether to activate change)

Step 5: Develop Change Requirements to Meet Performance Targets

  • If the architecture is not delivering the expected business value, develop requirements for changes
  • These requirements feed into either: minor architecture updates (within Phase H) or new ADM cycles (Phase A)
  • Connect performance measurement (Step 1) to change requirements — if KPIs are missed, something must change

Step 6: Manage Governance Process

  • Ensure the Architecture Board remains active and effective
  • Process incoming change requests, dispensation requests, and compliance issues
  • Update Architecture Contracts that are affected by changes to the architecture
  • Maintain the Governance Log with all decisions made

Step 7: Activate the Process to Implement Change

  • Based on the analysis in Step 4, decide the appropriate response:
Change received in Phase H:
         │
         ▼
    Classify the change
         │
    ┌────┴────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                             │
    ▼                                             ▼
MINOR CHANGE                              SIGNIFICANT CHANGE
(cosmetic, low impact,                    (affects architecture
within architecture                        baseline materially)
principles)                                      │
    │                                    ┌────────┴────────┐
    ▼                                    │                 │
Handle within Phase H                   ▼                 ▼
(update documentation,             MANAGE IN          NEW ADM
enforce through                    CURRENT CYCLE      CYCLE
existing contracts)                (loop back to      (loop back
                                   Phase E or F        to Phase A)
                                   if re-planning
                                   needed)
Exam tip

This 3-way decision is a common exam question. Know that Phase H can result in: (1) no action / minor update within Phase H, (2) loop back to Phase E/F for re-planning, or (3) loop back to Phase A for a new full architecture initiative.

Key Inputs to Phase H

Input Source
Architecture Baseline (current deployed architecture) Result of Phase G
Architecture Vision Phase A
Architecture Definition Document Finalized in Phase F
Architecture Contract Phase F — may need amendment
Compliance Assessments Phase G
Change Requests From operations, business, or technology teams
Business and Technology environment changes External/internal triggers

Key Outputs of Phase H

Output What It Is Exam Importance
Architecture Updates Updated Architecture Baseline reflecting approved changes High
Changes to Architecture Framework and Principles If the architecture framework itself needs updating Medium
New Request for Architecture Work Issued when a new full ADM cycle is needed Very High
Statement of Architecture Work (updated) If scope or resources must change Medium
Architecture Contract (amended) Updated to reflect approved architectural changes High
Governance Log (updated) Record of all change decisions High

Change Management — Three Types of Change

Phase H distinguishes between three types of change:

Simplification Change (minor):

  • A change that makes the architecture simpler without materially affecting it
  • Example: retiring a redundant application that was already deprecated in the roadmap
  • Handled within Phase H — no new ADM cycle needed

Incremental Change (medium):

  • A change that extends or modifies the architecture but remains within the original scope and principles
  • Example: adding a new integration point between two systems not originally planned
  • May require looping back to Phase E or F for re-planning, or handled in Phase H if the Architecture Board approves

Re-architecting Change (major):

  • A change so significant that it requires fundamentally rethinking the architecture
  • Examples: major merger/acquisition, new regulatory framework, completely new business model
  • Requires a new ADM cycle starting from Phase A (or possibly Phase B if only the business architecture must change)
Exam tip

The decision between these change types is made by the Architecture Board in Phase H. The key question is: "Does this change require new architecture design?" If no → handle in Phase H. If yes → trigger a new ADM cycle.

Architecture Debt — An Important Phase H Concept

Architecture Debt (sometimes called technical debt at architecture level) refers to the accumulated deviations from the architecture baseline that have occurred over time — through approved dispensations, undocumented implementation changes, and emergency workarounds.

Architecture Debt accumulates when:

  • Dispensations are granted but never resolved
  • Emergency changes bypass the governance process
  • Implementation teams make small deviations that go unmonitored

Phase H's monitoring role (Steps 1-2) helps identify and manage architecture debt before it becomes so large that the architecture is no longer relevant.

Key Takeaway for Day 4 (Phase H)

Phase H is continuous — it never ends while the architecture is live. It monitors the deployed architecture for drift, evaluates change requests, and decides whether to handle changes within Phase H, loop back to Phase E/F, or initiate a new ADM cycle (Phase A). The three-way decision on change classification is a key exam topic.

Day 5: ADM Guidelines and Techniques (Part III)

What Part III Is

Part III of TOGAF 9.2 provides guidance on how to apply the ADM — techniques, approaches, and guidelines that support specific phases or run across multiple phases. This is not a new set of phases — it is the toolbox architects use while working through Phases A–H.

For the Level 1 exam, Part III is tested through scenario-based questions: "An architect is in Phase E and needs to assess organizational readiness — what technique should they use?" Knowing which technique applies where is the exam challenge.

ADM Iteration and Levels — Applying the ADM Flexibly

The ADM is not always linear. TOGAF explicitly supports iteration:

Type 1 — Architecture Context Iteration (Preliminary + Phase A):

  • Iterate between Preliminary Phase and Phase A as the architecture context is being established
  • Example: Initial scoping in Phase A reveals the scope needs to change → loop back to review Preliminary Phase foundations

Type 2 — Architecture Definition Iteration (Phases B, C, D):

  • Iterate through the architecture design phases as understanding develops
  • Example: Data Architecture work (Phase C) reveals a business process assumption (Phase B) was wrong → loop back to Phase B
  • This is common and expected — architecture discovery is iterative

Type 3 — Transition Planning Iteration (Phases E, F):

  • Iterate between Phase E and Phase F as implementation constraints affect the roadmap
  • Example: Phase F costing reveals a Work Package is too expensive → loop back to Phase E to resequence

ADM Application at Different Levels: The ADM is not just for enterprise-wide architecture. It can be applied at different levels of the Architecture Landscape:

Level ADM Application
Enterprise Architecture Full ADM, whole organization in scope
Segment Architecture ADM applied to a business unit or function (Segment Architecture)
Capability Architecture ADM applied to enabling capabilities: security, data management, integration
Solution Architecture Lightweight ADM for a specific project (not full enterprise ADM)

Multiple ADM cycles can run simultaneously at different levels. A Segment Architecture must be consistent with the Enterprise Architecture above it.

Business Transformation Readiness Assessment

Used primarily in Phase E (and can be revisited in Phase F and H), this technique assesses whether the organization is ready to actually implement the architecture.

It is not enough to design a great architecture — if the organization is not ready to change, the architecture will fail in delivery.

TOGAF defines readiness factors:

Readiness Factor What It Assesses
Vision Is there a shared, compelling vision of the future state across leadership?
Desire, Willingness, and Resolve Do people WANT to change, or are they just complying?
Need Is there a genuine, recognized need to change? (burning platform or attractive opportunity)
Business Case Is there a financially justified case for the investment?
Funding Is the budget actually available and committed?
Sponsorship and Leadership Is there active, visible sponsorship from senior leadership?
Governance Are the right governance structures in place to manage the change?
Accountability Are individuals accountable for delivering change outcomes?
Workable Approach and Executable Plan Is the plan realistic and achievable?
IT Capacity to Execute Does the IT function have the technical capability to deliver?
Enterprise Capacity to Execute Can the organization absorb this much change simultaneously?

How it works:

  • Each factor is rated: typically Red/Amber/Green or a numeric scale
  • Factors rated Red require mitigation plans before delivery begins
  • Low readiness scores may indicate the target architecture is too ambitious for the current transition cycle → revise the plan to be more incremental
Exam tip

Know this technique by name — "Business Transformation Readiness Assessment" — and know it's used in Phase E. Questions often ask: "Which technique is used to assess whether an organization is ready to implement the architecture?" → Business Transformation Readiness Assessment.

Risk Management in the ADM

TOGAF's approach to risk management is integrated throughout the ADM — it is not a separate, one-time activity.

Two key risk assessment points:

Initial Risk Assessment (Phase E):

  • Identify risks for each Work Package
  • Classify each risk by:
    • Probability (likelihood of occurring)
    • Impact (consequence if it occurs)
  • Assign a risk classification:
Classification Meaning
Catastrophic Failure of the business; organization-threatening
Critical Major harm; significant reduction in capability
Marginal Minor harm; limited impact on operations
Negligible Minimal impact; can be tolerated

Residual Risk Assessment (Phase F):

  • After identifying mitigation strategies, reassess the risk level
  • Residual risk = the risk that remains AFTER mitigation actions have been applied
  • All residual risks must be formally accepted by an appropriate authority (typically the Architecture Sponsor or Board)

Risk Mitigation Strategies:

  1. Avoid — change the plan to eliminate the risk (e.g., choose a different technology)
  2. Transfer — shift the risk to another party (e.g., insurance, contract terms with vendors)
  3. Mitigate — reduce the probability or impact (e.g., additional testing, redundant systems)
  4. Accept — consciously accept the risk because mitigation cost exceeds potential impact
Exam tip

Residual risk is what's left after mitigation. It must be accepted (formally signed off), not ignored. This formal acceptance is an important governance step.

Capability-Based Planning

Capability-Based Planning is a technique that focuses on planning architecture initiatives around what the organization needs to be CAPABLE of doing, rather than around what systems or technologies to build.

Connection to Business Architecture:

  • Phase B produces the Business Capability Map (what the org can do today and what it needs to be able to do)
  • Capability-Based Planning connects those capability gaps to Work Packages in Phase E
  • Rather than saying "build System X", it says "deliver capability Y, which requires System X, Data Z, and Process Change W"

The Capability Increment: A capability increment is a discrete, measurable improvement in organizational capability. Work Packages are designed to deliver capability increments — this ensures that each deliverable can be directly tied to a business benefit.

Business Strategy
    │
    ▼
Capability Gap (from Business Capability Map)
    │
    ▼
Capability Increment (planned improvement)
    │
    ▼
Work Package (the implementation work to deliver the increment)
    │
    ▼
Business Benefit (measurable improvement in organizational capability)
Exam tip

Capability-Based Planning ensures architecture is always tied back to business need. It is the bridge between Phase B's Business Capability Map and Phase E's Work Package definition.

Interoperability Requirements

Interoperability is the ability of systems, organizations, or architectures to work together and share information effectively.

TOGAF defines three levels of interoperability:

Level Description Example
Operational Interoperability Organizations or teams working together effectively Saudi Aramco and a contractor sharing data through agreed processes
Technical Interoperability Systems and technology components working together ERP system integrating with a financial reporting system via API
Political/Business Interoperability Agreements, governance, standards that enable interoperability Two organizations agreeing on common data standards

Interoperability requirements are first identified in Phase B (organizational interoperability) and refined through Phases C and D (technical interoperability).

In Phase E, interoperability requirements are consolidated — Step 5 of Phase E formally requires "Consolidate and Reconcile Interoperability Requirements" before finalizing the roadmap.

Architecture Patterns

An Architecture Pattern is a reusable solution to a commonly occurring architecture problem within a given context.

Examples of architecture patterns:

  • Master Data Management (MDM) — how to manage shared entities across multiple systems
  • Event-Driven Architecture — using events to decouple systems
  • Microservices — breaking monoliths into independently deployable services
  • API Gateway — a single entry point managing access to multiple backend services
  • Hub-and-Spoke Integration — central integration platform vs. point-to-point

Architecture Patterns are stored in the Reference Library layer of the Architecture Repository. They can be retrieved and applied in any ADM phase where the relevant problem arises.

Exam tip

Architecture Patterns promote reuse. They are different from Reference Models (which are pre-built architectures). A Pattern is a reusable solution template; a Reference Model is a more complete example architecture.

Migration Planning Techniques (Phases E and F)

TOGAF defines four specific techniques used to turn gap-analysis results into an actionable, sequenced migration plan. These appear in the syllabus and can be tested by name — know what each one does and which phase uses it.

1. Implementation Factor Assessment and Deduction Matrix

  • A catalogue of the factors that will affect the implementation and migration plan — risks, issues, assumptions, dependencies, actions, and impacts.
  • For each factor it records: the factor, a description, and the deduction (the consequence — what the plan must do about it).
  • Purpose: make sure nothing that could derail delivery is overlooked when sequencing the work.
  • Used in Phase E.
Factor Description Deduction
Skills shortage No in-house Kafka expertise Budget for training or hire a partner before WP-002
Regulatory deadline New data-residency law effective Q3 Data-migration work package must finish before Q3

2. Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix

  • Takes the gaps identified in the Phase B, C, and D gap analyses, consolidates them in one place, assigns a solution (an SBB or an action) to each, and records dependencies between them.
  • Purpose: the direct bridge from gaps → Work Packages. Related gaps with shared solutions/dependencies are grouped into a Work Package.
  • Used in Phase E.
Gap Architecture (B/C/D) Solution Dependency
No master customer record Data Implement MDM platform Requires CDM defined first
Manual order entry Business/App New order-capture application Requires MDM platform

3. Architecture Definition Increments Table

  • Shows the increments of capability delivered across the sequence of projects/Transition Architectures — i.e., what the organization can newly do after each step.
  • Purpose: tie each Transition Architecture to concrete, incremental business value.
  • Used in Phases E and F.

4. Transition Architectures State Evolution Table

  • Shows how each SBB/service evolves across the Transition Architectures — marking each as, e.g., new, transition, retained, or target at each transition state.
  • Purpose: make the state of every component explicit at every step, so nothing is stranded.
  • Used in Phases E and F.
Exam tip

Remember the pairing — the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions & Dependencies Matrix turns gaps into Work Packages; the Implementation Factor Assessment & Deduction Matrix captures risks/issues/dependencies that shape the plan; the Architecture Definition Increments Table and Transition Architectures State Evolution Table describe how capability and components evolve across Transition Architectures. All four are Phase E/F migration-planning techniques. (These carry over essentially unchanged into the 10th Edition's "Applying the ADM" content.)

Key Takeaway for Day 5 (ADM Techniques)

Part III provides the toolbox for the ADM. The most exam-tested techniques are: Business Transformation Readiness Assessment (Phase E), Risk Management with Residual Risk (Phases E, F), Capability-Based Planning (Phases B, E), Interoperability Requirements (Phases B, C, D, E), and the four Migration Planning techniques (Implementation Factor Assessment & Deduction Matrix; Consolidated Gaps, Solutions & Dependencies Matrix; Architecture Definition Increments Table; Transition Architectures State Evolution Table — all Phase E/F). Know which technique is used in which phase — this is how exam questions are framed.

Day 6: Architecture Governance (Part VII) and Content Framework (Part IV)

Section A: Architecture Governance (Part VII)

What Architecture Governance Is

Architecture Governance is the practice and orientation by which enterprise architectures and other architectures are managed and controlled at an enterprise-wide level. It ensures that:

  • Architecture decisions are made consistently and appropriately
  • Architecture is aligned with business strategy
  • Implementations conform to the architecture
  • Architecture evolves in a controlled manner

Without governance, architecture becomes aspirational documentation that nobody follows. Governance is what makes architecture real.

The Architecture Governance Framework

The Architecture Governance Framework, established in the Preliminary Phase, consists of:

  1. Architecture Board — the governance body that makes decisions
  2. Architecture Compliance Reviews — the process for checking conformance
  3. Architecture Contracts — the formal agreements that enforce architecture
  4. Architecture Dispensations (Waivers) — the mechanism for formally permitting exceptions
  5. Governance Log — the permanent audit record of all governance decisions

The Architecture Board

The Architecture Board is the governance body responsible for overseeing the architecture practice and making authoritative architecture decisions.

Composition:

  • Chief Architect (typically chairs)
  • Enterprise Architects
  • Domain Architects (one per domain, or as appropriate)
  • Business representatives (senior business stakeholders)
  • IT representatives (CIO, IT leadership)
  • Project representatives (rotating, for current initiatives)
  • Potentially: external advisors, security officer, compliance officer

Responsibilities of the Architecture Board:

Responsibility Description
Approve architecture strategies and policies Set the direction for the architecture practice
Maintain consistency Ensure architectures across projects are consistent with each other and with enterprise principles
Provide guidance and arbitration Resolve architecture conflicts between projects or domains
Approve Architecture Change Requests Decide whether changes to the baseline architecture are accepted
Grant Dispensations Formally permit exceptions to the architecture (with conditions)
Monitor conformance Oversee Compliance Assessments and ensure non-conformances are resolved
Ensure reuse Identify opportunities to reuse architecture assets across projects
Manage the Governance Log Maintain records of all architecture decisions
Exam tip

The Architecture Board is a COMMITTEE, not an individual. It is the highest architecture authority — even the Chief Architect cannot unilaterally override the Architecture Board. All major architecture decisions (approvals, dispensations, change requests) flow through the Board.

Architecture Compliance Reviews

A Compliance Review is a formal assessment of how well a project's solution conforms to the target architecture, conducted by or on behalf of the Architecture Board.

Types of Reviews:

  • Formal Review — complete review by the Architecture Board; used for major projects or significant architecture decisions
  • Informal Review (desk review) — lightweight check for smaller projects or incremental changes

When Compliance Reviews occur:

  • At project milestones (e.g., at design completion, before build, before go-live)
  • At architecture decision points
  • On a regular schedule (e.g., quarterly reviews of all active projects)
  • When a project requests a dispensation

The Compliance Assessment output: The Compliance Assessment documents:

  • Which aspects of the architecture were assessed
  • The compliance level for each aspect (see the spectrum below)
  • Recommended actions for non-conformant areas
  • Formal sign-off by the Architecture Board

Architecture Compliance Spectrum:

STRONGEST ◄─────────────────────────────────────────────► WEAKEST
                                                     
Fully       Conformant   Compliant   Consistent   Irrelevant   Non-
Conformant                                                     conformant
    │            │           │           │            │           │
Full         All        Some        Same          Not       Conflicts
alignment    aspects    aspects     terminology   relevant  with the
with ALL     align      not         only          at all    architecture
aspects                 covered
Exam tip

Know the 6 levels in order. "Conformant" and "Fully Conformant" are both positive — the difference is completeness. "Non-conformant" is the danger zone — it must be resolved. "Irrelevant" is not a negative — it means the architecture simply doesn't apply to this part of the solution.

Architecture Dispensations (Waivers)

A Dispensation (sometimes called a Waiver) is formal permission for a project to deviate from the architecture. It is NOT the same as ignoring the architecture.

When a Dispensation is needed:

  • A project cannot conform to the architecture due to technical constraints
  • A vendor product doesn't support the required standards
  • Time or cost pressure makes strict conformance impractical
  • The architecture itself may have an error that is being worked on

The Dispensation process:

  1. Project team identifies a non-conformance
  2. Project team submits a formal Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board
  3. Dispensation Request includes: what the deviation is, why it's necessary, what the risks are, what compensating controls are in place
  4. Architecture Board reviews and decides: approve, approve with conditions, or reject
  5. If approved, the dispensation is time-limited — it has an expiry date and conditions that must be met
  6. All dispensations are recorded in the Governance Log
  7. Dispensations should be resolved before they expire — either the architecture is updated, or the solution is brought into conformance
Exam tip

Dispensations are FORMAL, TIME-LIMITED, and recorded in the Governance Log. They are not permanent exceptions — every dispensation has a resolution plan. "Project X has a dispensation to use Oracle database instead of the standard PostgreSQL; the dispensation expires in 12 months when the project is expected to migrate" is a typical dispensation scenario.

The Governance Log

The Governance Log is a Layer 6 element of the Architecture Repository. It records:

  • All Architecture Board decisions (approvals, rejections)
  • All Dispensations granted (with conditions and expiry dates)
  • All Compliance Assessment results
  • All Architecture Change Requests (pending, approved, rejected)
  • Architecture contract status
  • Architecture Review minutes

The Governance Log is the audit trail of the architecture governance function. It ensures:

  • Accountability — decisions can be traced back to who made them and when
  • Learning — patterns in dispensations reveal architecture weaknesses
  • Compliance evidence — demonstrates to regulators and auditors that governance is real
Exam tip

The Governance Log is in Layer 6 of the Architecture Repository (the deepest layer). It is maintained throughout the entire ADM — from Preliminary Phase through Phase H. It is never deleted or archived — it is the permanent record.

Section B: Architecture Content Framework (Part IV)

What Part IV Defines

Part IV of TOGAF 9.2 defines the structured taxonomy of what architecture produces. It answers: "What exactly should we be creating when we do enterprise architecture?"

The Content Framework introduces three levels of content:

DELIVERABLES
    │ (contain)
    ▼
ARTIFACTS
    │ (describe)
    ▼
BUILDING BLOCKS

Deliverables

A Deliverable is a work product that is contractually specified and formally reviewed, agreed upon, and signed off by stakeholders.

Deliverables are the major formal outputs of ADM phases — the documents that are approved and baselined.

Key Deliverable Produced In What It Contains
Architecture Vision Phase A High-level target state description
Statement of Architecture Work Phase A Project charter
Architecture Definition Document (ADD) Phases B, C, D (finalized F) All 4 domains, baseline and target
Architecture Requirements Specification Phases B, C, D (finalized F) Measurable requirements
Architecture Roadmap Phase E (finalized F) Sequenced work plan
Implementation and Migration Plan Phase E (finalized F) Detailed delivery plan
Architecture Contract Phase F Compliance agreement
Compliance Assessment Phase G Conformance evaluation
Exam tip

Deliverables are FORMAL — they are signed off, version-controlled, and baselined. When a deliverable is updated, it goes through a change control process.

Artifacts

An Artifact is a work product that describes an architectural aspect. Artifacts are the building blocks of deliverables — the ADD, for example, is a deliverable that contains many artifacts.

TOGAF classifies all architecture artifacts into exactly three types:

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   ARTIFACT TYPES (3)                      │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CATALOG             MATRIX              DIAGRAM          │
│  Lists of things     Relationships       Visual           │
│  of the same type    between things      representations  │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Application         Application/        Business Process  │
│  Catalog             Business Function   Diagram           │
│                      Matrix                               │
│  Technology          Data Entity/        Application       │
│  Standards           Business Function   Communication     │
│  Catalog             Matrix              Diagram           │
│                                                           │
│  Business            Role/Actor          Infrastructure    │
│  Service Catalog     Matrix              Diagram           │
│                                                           │
│  Data Entity         Stakeholder/        Value Chain       │
│  Catalog             Value Driver        Diagram           │
│                      Matrix                               │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Exam tip

This is heavily tested. "Which type of artifact shows the relationship between applications and business functions?" → Matrix (specifically the Application/Business Function Matrix). "Which type of artifact shows all approved technology standards?" → Catalog (Technology Standards Catalog). "Which type of artifact provides a visual representation of a business process?" → Diagram (Business Process Diagram).

Key examples to know:

Artifact Type What It Shows
Application Catalog Catalog List of all applications with status
Technology Standards Catalog Catalog Approved technologies by category
Data Entity Catalog Catalog All data entities in the organization
Application/Business Function Matrix Matrix Which applications support which functions
Data Entity/Business Function Matrix Matrix Which data entities are used by which functions
Role/Actor Matrix Matrix Which roles play which parts in processes
Business Process Diagram (BPMN) Diagram Steps and flow of a business process
Application Communication Diagram Diagram How applications interact
Infrastructure Diagram Diagram Physical/virtual infrastructure layout
Value Chain Diagram Diagram Porter's value chain representation
Organizational Map Diagram Org structure and relationships

Building Blocks (Revisited in Context of Part IV)

Part IV formally defines Building Blocks as packages of functionality with defined interfaces. The distinction between ABBs and SBBs is a Part IV concept:

Architecture Building Block (ABB):

  • Captures architecture requirements (conceptual)
  • Technology-independent
  • Defined in the target architecture design phases (B, C, D)
  • Specifies WHAT is needed without specifying HOW it is implemented
  • Example: "A payment processing service that accepts multiple payment methods and returns a confirmation"

Solution Building Block (SBB):

  • Represents a component that will implement an ABB (concrete)
  • Technology-specific
  • Defined during implementation planning (Phase E onward)
  • Specifies the specific product, system, or component
  • Example: "Stripe Payment Gateway v3 API" implements the "payment processing service" ABB

Building Blocks in the Architecture Repository: Building Blocks (especially SBBs once proven in delivery) are stored in the Reference Library layer of the Architecture Repository. Future projects can reuse them rather than reinventing solutions.

Architecture Content Metamodel

The Content Metamodel (defined in Part IV) is a model of models — it defines the structure and relationships between all architecture content entities.

It includes entities across all 4 domains:

Domain Key Metamodel Entities
Business Actor, Role, Organization Unit, Function, Service, Process, Event, Business Capability
Data Data Entity, Logical Data Component, Physical Data Component
Application Application Component, Application Function, Application Interaction, Interface
Technology Node, Platform Service, Technology Component, Network
Exam tip

For Level 1, you do not need to know the metamodel in detail. You need to know: (a) the metamodel exists as Part of the Content Framework; (b) it defines the relationships between entities across all 4 domains; (c) it is used to ensure architecture artifacts are consistent with each other.

Key Takeaway for Day 6 (Governance + Content Framework)

Architecture Governance (Part VII) makes architecture real through the Architecture Board, Compliance Assessments, Architecture Contracts, Dispensations, and the Governance Log. The 6 compliance levels from Fully Conformant to Non-conformant are exam essentials. The Content Framework (Part IV) defines Deliverables (formal sign-off documents), Artifacts (three types: Catalogs, Matrices, Diagrams), and Building Blocks (ABBs and SBBs). Know the three artifact types and be able to classify examples.

Additional terms introduced this week:
