Week 3 Practice Quiz

30 Questions | Time: 45 minutes | Passing score: 24/30 (80%)

Preliminary Phase Questions (Q1–Q5)

Q1. Which of the following BEST describes the primary purpose of the Preliminary Phase in TOGAF?

A) To initiate a specific architecture project and produce an Architecture Vision
B) To establish the organization's architecture capability, governance, and principles before any architecture project begins
C) To plan the migration of systems from the current to the target architecture
D) To monitor the implemented architecture for changes

Answer: B — The Preliminary Phase sets up the architecture capability (the ability to do architecture) for the whole organization. It runs before any specific project (Phase A) begins. Phase A initiates specific projects; Phase F handles migration planning; Phase H handles monitoring.

Q2. Architecture Principles established in the Preliminary Phase have four formal components. Which combination below correctly lists all four?

A) Name, Description, Owner, Approval Date
B) Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications
C) Title, Objective, Justification, Implementation
D) Label, Rule, Benefit, Exceptions

Answer: B — The four components are: Name (label), Statement (the rule), Rationale (why it matters, business benefit), Implications (what following it requires from business and IT). These exact names appear in exam questions.

Q3. What is the output of the Preliminary Phase that describes how TOGAF has been adapted to fit the organization's culture, methods, and terminology?

A) Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture
B) Architecture Governance Framework
C) Tailored Architecture Framework
D) Architecture Principles Document

Answer: C — The Tailored Architecture Framework is TOGAF customized to the organization. It includes adapted terminology, selected techniques, tool choices, and integrated Architecture Principles. It is a core output of the Preliminary Phase.

Q4. An organization is implementing TOGAF for the first time. The team has completed the Preliminary Phase. What is the MOST appropriate next action?

A) Begin developing the Business Architecture
B) Issue a Request for Architecture Work to initiate Phase A for the first architecture project
C) Perform a Gap Analysis to identify what the organization lacks
D) Create an Architecture Contract with the project delivery teams

Answer: B — After the Preliminary Phase, the first architecture initiative is started by issuing a Request for Architecture Work, which triggers Phase A. The Preliminary Phase sets up the framework; Phase A starts the first project within that framework.

Q5. Which layer of the Architecture Repository is set up in the Preliminary Phase to store all future architecture decisions, dispensations, and compliance results?

A) Reference Library
B) Architecture Landscape
C) Standards Information Base
D) Governance Log

Answer: D — The Governance Log (Layer 6) is the audit trail for all governance decisions. It is established in the Preliminary Phase and maintained throughout the entire ADM. The Reference Library stores reference architectures and patterns; the Architecture Landscape stores actual architectures.

Phase F Questions (Q6–Q10)

Q6. Phase F "Migration Planning" is BEST distinguished from Phase E "Opportunities & Solutions" by which of the following?

A) Phase F designs the architecture; Phase E plans the implementation
B) Phase F identifies Work Packages; Phase E defines Transition Architectures
C) Phase E produces strategic plans at Version 0.1; Phase F finalizes detailed plans with resource commitments, costs, and Architecture Contracts
D) Phase F is only needed for large organizations; Phase E is sufficient for small organizations

Answer: C — Phase E produces Version 0.1 of the Architecture Roadmap and Migration Plan (strategic, high-level). Phase F finalizes both with detailed resource commitments, cost-benefit analysis, prioritization, and creates Architecture Contracts. Both phases work on the same output documents but at different levels of detail.

Q7. Which of the following is a formal deliverable produced in Phase F that was NOT produced in Phase E?

A) Work Package list
B) Architecture Roadmap
C) Architecture Contracts
D) Transition Architectures

Answer: C — Architecture Contracts are created in Phase F. Work Packages and Transition Architectures are defined in Phase E. The Architecture Roadmap exists in both phases but at different levels of maturity (v0.1 in E, finalized in F).

Q8. In Phase F Step 4, the architect must prioritize Work Packages using a Cost/Benefit Assessment. A Work Package is assessed as HIGH business value and HIGH implementation risk. What is the recommended approach?

A) Implement first — the high value justifies the risk
B) Eliminate — high risk makes it not worth doing
C) Implement with risk mitigation strategies in place
D) Defer indefinitely until risk decreases

Answer: C — High value + high risk → implement with mitigation. The risk must be managed through appropriate mitigation strategies (proof-of-concept, additional testing, phased rollout) rather than abandoning the work package or ignoring the risk.

Q9. An Architecture Contract is BEST described as:

A) An employment contract between the Chief Architect and the organization
B) A formal agreement between the architecture team and implementation parties on deliverables, quality, and conformance to the architecture
C) A legal agreement between the organization and a software vendor
D) An internal document recording Architecture Board decisions

Answer: B — An Architecture Contract is a formal agreement between the architecture team (or Architecture Board) and those delivering implementations (project teams, system integrators, vendors). It specifies what will be delivered, the quality standards, and the required conformance to the architecture.

Q10. Phase F Step 7 requires completing the architecture development cycle and documenting lessons learned. Where are these lessons learned stored for use in future ADM cycles?

A) Architecture Landscape layer of the Architecture Repository
B) Governance Log layer of the Architecture Repository
C) Reference Library layer of the Architecture Repository
D) Standards Information Base layer of the Architecture Repository

Answer: C — Lessons Learned are stored in the Reference Library (Layer 5 of the Architecture Repository). The Reference Library contains reference architectures, patterns, guidelines, and lessons from previous cycles. The Governance Log (Layer 6) stores governance decisions.

Phase G Questions (Q11–Q15)

Q11. What is the PRIMARY purpose of Phase G — Implementation Governance?

A) To design the target architecture for all 4 domains
B) To ensure that what gets built during implementation conforms to the agreed architecture
C) To plan the migration from the current to the target architecture
D) To manage ongoing changes to the architecture after go-live

Answer: B — Phase G's primary purpose is governance of implementation — ensuring conformance. Phase A–D design the architecture; Phase F plans the migration; Phase H manages post-go-live changes.

Q12. An architecture compliance review reveals that a project's solution deviates from the target architecture in ways that are NOT acceptable and actively conflict with the architecture. Which compliance level applies?

A) Consistent
B) Compliant
C) Irrelevant
D) Non-conformant

Answer: D — Non-conformant means the solution actively conflicts with the architecture. This is the most serious outcome of a compliance review. It requires resolution: either change the solution, request a dispensation, or revise the architecture.

Q13. During Phase G, a project team discovers that the approved target architecture requires a feature that a chosen software product does not support. Implementing a workaround would mean deviating from the architecture. What is the CORRECT next step according to TOGAF?

A) Proceed with the workaround without notifying the architecture team
B) Cancel the project and start over from Phase A
C) Submit a formal Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board, explaining the deviation and its justification
D) Redesign the architecture unilaterally to accommodate the limitation

Answer: C — The correct process is to submit a formal Dispensation Request. The Architecture Board reviews the request and grants or denies a time-limited waiver. Proceeding without notification violates governance; cancelling is disproportionate; unilateral architecture changes bypass the governance process.

Q14. A project has delivered a system that uses the same architectural terminology and concepts as the target architecture, but the system has no direct relationship to the target architecture and neither conforms nor conflicts with it. What is the compliance level?

A) Conformant
B) Compliant
C) Consistent
D) Irrelevant

Answer: C — Consistent — the solution uses the same terminology and concepts but has no direct relationship to the architecture. It neither conforms to nor conflicts with the architecture. This is different from Irrelevant (where the architecture simply doesn't apply to this solution at all).

Q15. Which Phase G output is described as a formal evaluation document assessing how well an implementation project conforms to the target architecture, produced after a formal review by or on behalf of the Architecture Board?

A) Architecture Vision
B) Compliance Assessment
C) Statement of Architecture Work
D) Implementation and Migration Plan

Answer: B — The Compliance Assessment is the key Phase G output. It documents which aspects were assessed, the compliance level for each, and recommended actions. It is produced as a result of the Architecture Compliance Review.

Phase H Questions (Q16–Q20)

Q16. Which of the following BEST describes the nature of Phase H compared to Phases A through G?

A) Phase H is a one-time phase that runs after go-live and then ends
B) Phase H is continuous — it runs indefinitely while the architecture is live, monitoring and managing changes
C) Phase H runs simultaneously with Phase A for every new project
D) Phase H is optional — small organizations can skip it

Answer: B — Phase H is continuous. Unlike Phases A–G which are episodic (they run for a project and complete), Phase H is the ongoing operational state of the architecture after delivery. It never "ends" while the architecture is in use.

Q17. A Phase H analysis of the deployed architecture reveals that a small, localized change is needed to improve system performance in one area, without affecting the architecture baseline or requiring any new architecture design work. How should this be handled?

A) Initiate a new full ADM cycle starting from Phase A
B) Return to Phase E to redefine Work Packages
C) Handle the change within Phase H as a simplification change
D) Raise an Architecture Change Request for Architecture Board review

Answer: C — A minor change that doesn't materially affect the architecture baseline is a "simplification change" handled within Phase H. New ADM cycles are for significant changes requiring new architecture design. Phase E loops are for medium-scope changes affecting planning.

Q18. Which of the following is a TECHNOLOGY TRIGGER that would activate Phase H change management activity?

A) The organization announces a merger with a competitor
B) A major vendor announces that a database platform used in the current architecture will reach end-of-life in 18 months
C) The Architecture Board decides to update Architecture Principles
D) A project team requests an additional Work Package for a new feature

Answer: B — Technology end-of-life is a classic technology trigger for Phase H. The architecture must be assessed to determine how the EOL technology will be replaced. Option A is a business trigger (not technology). Option C is an architecture governance trigger. Option D is a project delivery issue for Phase G.

Q19. Which of the following Phase H outputs formally initiates a NEW full ADM cycle when a change is too significant to be handled within Phase H?

A) Architecture Contract (amended)
B) Architecture Updates
C) New Request for Architecture Work
D) Compliance Assessment

Answer: C — A New Request for Architecture Work is the Phase H output that triggers Phase A of a new ADM cycle. This is the formal mechanism for initiating a major new architecture initiative in response to a significant business or technology change.

Q20. "Architecture Debt" refers to which of the following in TOGAF context?

A) The financial cost of the architecture program
B) Architecture deliverables that have not yet been produced
C) The accumulated deviations from the architecture baseline through dispensations, undocumented changes, and emergency workarounds
D) Outdated documentation that no longer reflects the current architecture

Answer: C — Architecture Debt is the accumulation of deviations from the architecture baseline. Like technical debt in software, it grows when shortcuts are taken (emergency workarounds, unresolved dispensations) and must be actively managed to prevent the architecture from becoming irrelevant.

Architecture Governance Questions (Q21–Q25)

Q21. Which of the following BEST describes the Architecture Board's role regarding Architecture Change Requests during Phase G?

A) The Architecture Board is not involved in Phase G — that is managed by project managers
B) The Architecture Board reviews and approves or rejects Architecture Change Requests raised when implementation projects discover non-conformances
C) The Architecture Board implements the changes itself
D) The Architecture Board can approve changes without documenting them in the Governance Log

Answer: B — The Architecture Board is the final authority on Architecture Change Requests. All requests (whether raised in Phase G or Phase H) must go through the Board. All decisions are recorded in the Governance Log.

Q22. A project has been granted a Dispensation (Waiver) from the Architecture Board to use a non-standard database platform. The dispensation has been running for 14 months and is approaching its 18-month expiry. What should happen at expiry?

A) The dispensation automatically renews until the project is complete
B) The project must be cancelled
C) The dispensation must be resolved: either the architecture is updated to accommodate the database, or the project migrates to the standard database
D) The Architecture Board chairman can verbally extend the dispensation without documentation

Answer: C — Dispensations are time-limited with an expected resolution. At expiry, the deviation must be resolved — either the architecture formally accepts the exception (updating the architecture baseline) or the project conforms to the original architecture. All resolutions are documented in the Governance Log.

Q23. Which layer of the Architecture Repository contains the permanent record of all Architecture Board decisions, dispensations granted, and compliance assessment results?

A) Reference Library (Layer 5)
B) Architecture Landscape (Layer 3)
C) Architecture Capability (Layer 2)
D) Governance Log (Layer 6)

Answer: D — The Governance Log (Layer 6) is the permanent audit trail for all governance decisions. It is established in the Preliminary Phase and maintained throughout the entire ADM lifecycle.

Q24. A project solution uses the same vocabulary and concepts as the target architecture, conforms to most aspects of the architecture, but some architecture aspects are simply not addressed by the solution (neither conforming nor conflicting). What is the BEST compliance level to assign?

A) Consistent
B) Compliant
C) Conformant
D) Fully Conformant

Answer: B — Compliant — the solution addresses most aspects and doesn't conflict with anything, but some architecture aspects are simply not applicable or addressed. "Conformant" would require ALL relevant aspects to be addressed. "Consistent" only means same terminology with no direct relationship. "Compliant" captures "mostly aligned, some gaps but no conflicts."

Q25. Which of the following is NOT a responsibility of the Architecture Board?

A) Approving architecture strategies and policies
B) Granting dispensations for architecture deviations
C) Designing the solution architecture for individual projects
D) Monitoring conformance to the enterprise architecture

Answer: C — The Architecture Board does NOT design solutions. That is the role of architects and solution delivery teams. The Architecture Board governs, reviews, approves, and arbitrates — it does not do architecture design work.

ADM Techniques and Content Framework Questions (Q26–Q30)

Q26. An architect is in Phase E and needs to assess whether the organization has the organizational culture, leadership, and capacity to implement a major transformation. Which TOGAF technique should be used?

A) Gap Analysis
B) Business Transformation Readiness Assessment
C) Business Scenarios
D) Capability-Based Planning

Answer: B — The Business Transformation Readiness Assessment is specifically designed to evaluate organizational readiness for transformation. It assesses factors including vision, desire, leadership, funding, governance, and capacity. Gap Analysis compares architectures; Business Scenarios develop Architecture Vision; Capability-Based Planning links capabilities to Work Packages.

Q27. Risk Management in TOGAF distinguishes between the "Initial Risk Assessment" and "Residual Risk." What is "Residual Risk"?

A) The risk that was identified but deemed too small to address
B) The risk remaining after all mitigation strategies have been applied
C) The total risk before any mitigation is considered
D) Risk that was incorrectly classified in the initial assessment

Answer: B — Residual Risk is what remains after mitigation strategies are in place. Even after accepting a risk or mitigating it, some risk always remains. Residual Risk must be formally accepted by an appropriate authority (Architecture Sponsor or Architecture Board) — it cannot simply be ignored.

Q28. A Data Entity/Business Function Matrix shows the relationship between data entities and business functions. Using TOGAF's Content Framework classification, what TYPE of artifact is this?

A) Catalog
B) Matrix
C) Diagram
D) Deliverable

Answer: B — A Matrix shows relationships between two (or more) categories of things. A Catalog is a list of things of the same type. A Diagram is a visual/graphical representation. A Deliverable is a signed-off work product that contains artifacts.

Q29. Which of the following correctly identifies the difference between an Architecture Building Block (ABB) and a Solution Building Block (SBB)?

A) ABBs are used in Technology Architecture; SBBs are used in Business Architecture
B) ABBs are conceptual and technology-independent (defining WHAT is needed); SBBs are concrete and technology-specific (defining WHAT will implement it)
C) ABBs are created during implementation; SBBs are created during architecture design
D) SBBs are always larger than ABBs in scope

Answer: B — ABBs define the architectural requirement conceptually ("a message brokering service"). SBBs name the specific implementation ("Apache Kafka 3.x"). ABBs are designed in Phases B–D; SBBs are identified/built in Phases E onward. ABBs are in any domain; SBBs are always implementation-specific.

Q30. An architect needs to show which organizational roles participate in each step of a business process. Which combination of artifact type and name is MOST appropriate?

A) Catalog — Business Service Catalog
B) Diagram — Business Process Diagram (with swim lanes showing roles)
C) Matrix — Role/Actor Matrix
D) Deliverable — Architecture Definition Document

Answer: B — A Business Process Diagram with swim lanes is the standard way to show which roles perform which steps in a process. Swim lanes visually separate the activities of each actor/role. A Role/Actor Matrix (option C) shows which actors play which roles but doesn't show the process flow or sequence. Option B is the better answer for showing WHICH ROLE does WHAT STEP in a process.
